newsitem.title: USA: Consumers find filing bankruptcy easy, Visa says.
newsitem.headline: Consumers find filing bankruptcy easy, Visa says.

text.p: Credit card giant Visa, pressing hard for tighter bankruptcy laws, released a survey Wednesday that showed most people who have filed found the process "easy."
"It's clear that too often the bankruptcy system is seen as an easy escape, when in fact it leads to a whole new set of barricades," said Kenneth Crone, Visa senior vice president.
Asked if filing bankruptcy was an easy process, about 66 percent of the 3,500 respondents said "yes." About 27 percent said they would consider filing again.
The non-scientific survey, written by Visa staff, was mailed last November to 50,000 people who filed for bankruptcy during the previous 12 months.
Crone noted that less of half of the respondents, about 45 percent, said they sought professional debt counseling prior to considering bankruptcy.
"Increased consumer education will help people realize that bankruptcy should be a last resort instead of a first option," Crone said.
With over one million consumer bankruptcies last year and late payments on credit cards also setting records, Visa and other credit card companies have lobbied Congress to change the bankruptcy laws.
The bankruptcies and delinquiencies have already hurt profits at some companies.

Advanta Corp shocked the market last month when it announced it would report a net loss for the first quarter. But not all are suffering as MBNA Corp reported Wednesday its net profit rose 34 percent in the first quarter.
Consumer advocates said they also supported greater use of credit counseling, but denied that lax bankruptcy laws were responsible for current predicament of credit card companies.
"They have largely created the problem," said Stephen Brobeck, executive director of Consumer Federation of America. "They can control 95 percent of this problem by more prudently extending credit."
Visa's survey found 11 percent of respondents had filed for bankruptcy more than once. Most of the respondents were between 26 and 50 years old.

Asked what was the "last straw" that led to a bankruptcy filing, about 30 percent cited harrassment from bill collectors. Unemployment was cited by 12 percent and medical reasons by another 11 percent.
